title: Prices Keep Climbing: What the New Inflation Report Means
summary:
Prices went up again last month, and the latest inflation report has little good news for families. The Consumer Price Index showed prices rose four-tenths of a percent, driven largely by higher food and energy costs. Housing costs also climbed three-tenths of a percent, accounting for roughly a third of the larger-than-expected monthly increase. Economists now expect inflation to run at about 4 percent for the year, outpacing wage growth and squeezing household budgets further.

Inflation means prices rising over time. When it stays high, the money in your pocket buys less than it did before. The Federal Reserve, America's central bank, aims for 2 percent inflation. The latest report came in hotter than many economists expected.

Austan Goolsbee, president of the Federal Reserve Bank of Chicago, called it 'another distressing report, borderline disturbing.' He said several things that were supposed to have stopped pushing up costs are still going. The war in the Middle East has led to higher energy prices, and the impact of tariffs on goods prices was supposed to have faded by now. It still continues.

Perhaps the most troubling part, Goolsbee said, is that services inflation — including health care and many other services — is not coming down. Unlike energy prices, it is probably not mostly driven by oil prices or tariffs or things that might pass quickly. 'We have got a real inflation issue on our hands that has been developing, and we're going to have to deal with that,' he said.

Food and housing costs keep climbing, and unlike other expenses, these are not things families can simply cut out of their budgets. Goolsbee says the problem is on everyone's mind in the Midwest, from businesses and nonprofits to ordinary shoppers. He said a farmer in downstate Illinois even sent him a diesel pump, saying prices are killing them.

A newer factor is demand from the AI build-out. Data centers costing trillions of dollars are pushing up the cost of construction, computers, electrical equipment, and computer chips. Goolsbee said this demand is almost like a stimulus — extra spending that heats up the economy. At the Fed, the main tool is interest rates, and higher rates have made some players in that space respond. His fear is that the overheating could spread beyond AI-related sectors into the prices of a whole bunch of things.

The job market, meanwhile, has been pretty steady. The law gives the Fed two jobs: keep prices stable and maximize employment. The employment side is doing pretty well. The inflation side is not. Inflation has remained above the Fed's 2 percent target for nearly six years now, raising a worry that businesses and consumers may start accepting high inflation as the new normal.
why_it_matters: When prices rise faster than pay, families have less money for the things they need, so inflation touches everyday life.

keywords.explanation: Inflation means prices keep rising over time.
The Consumer Price Index is a report that tracks how prices change.
Tariffs are extra taxes on goods brought in from other countries.
A stimulus is extra spending that heats up the economy.
The Federal Reserve is America's central bank, which works to keep prices stable.

background_read: Inflation is what happens when prices rise over time, so the same amount of money buys less than it used to.
In the United States, the Federal Reserve is the central bank, and one of its jobs is to keep inflation near 2 percent by using tools such as interest rates.
When prices for food, energy, and housing climb faster than pay, families feel squeezed, because those are costs they cannot simply skip.
Economists watch a monthly report called the Consumer Price Index to see how fast prices are changing and whether inflation is getting better or worse.
